title: AI maturity in marketing: What the research reveals
content:
AI maturity explains why 98% of marketing teams now use AI in some way, yet only 10% report transformational results, according to our 2026 State of AI in Marketing research . AI maturity measures how consistently a customer-facing team turns AI into measurable business outcomes, and it matters more than the number of tools or pilots you’ve launched.
So if your team has tools, pilots, and plenty of enthusiasm but can't yet point to the revenue or customer experience gains, you're not alone. Adoption is mostly solved, but the gap is impact — and closing it starts with knowing where you stand.
This guide defines the four AI maturity stages (Early, Emerging, Established, and Transformational), shows how to run an AI maturity assessment, and maps each stage to a next step with Loop Marketing. If you want the benchmarks first, download the 2026 State of AI in Marketing Report .
AI maturity measures how consistently a go-to-market team turns AI into measurable business outcomes. For marketing, that means AI runs in documented workflows, draws on clean customer data, operates under human oversight, and ties to metrics like MQLs, customer acquisition cost (CAC), and revenue. Sales and service use the same definition with different workflows and metrics.
Maturity beats counting pilots because pilots measure activity and maturity measures repeatability. A team can run ten experiments and still sit at the bottom of the curve if none connect to the CRM, have an owner, or show a before-and-after result.
Marketing leads to other GTM functions, with 42% of marketers reporting advanced AI use (Established or Transformational), compared with 27% in sales and 23% in service. For those functions, see the sales maturity model and the customer success maturity model .
The four stages come from HubSpot’s research. The six-dimension scoring later in this guide is an editorial framework, not an official HubSpot metric. Treat all benchmarks as directional.
An AI maturity model includes stages that run from experimentation to scaled activation.
The four AI maturity levels distinguish Early, Emerging, Established, and Transformational adoption patterns. A team can sit at different levels in different workflows, so score the workflow first.
The payoff at the top is measurable: 96% of Transformational adopters met or exceeded their MQL targets, and they were roughly 3.5x more likely to outperform CAC targets . Among all marketers surveyed, 72% said AI makes it easier to hit revenue and MQL targets, and about 65% said the same for CAC goals. These results are self-reported, so treat them as directional benchmarks.
Most AI maturity models agree that capability builds in stages. They differ in scope: the two best-known references cover whole enterprises, while HubSpot’s stages describe marketing adoption.
Roughly, Early matches Gartner’s Foundational, Emerging matches Emerging, Established spans Operational and Scaled, and Transformational matches the top stage in both models. The criteria differ, so use the mapping for orientation, not score conversion.
An AI maturity assessment combines evidence about use cases, data access, workflow integration, governance, and outcomes. Proof means the workflow, the data source, the owner, and the result.
Don’t equate self-reported maturity with measured performance. A team that rates itself Transformational without measurement in place hasn’t shown anything yet.
A marketing operations or revenue operations lead usually has the right mix of process knowledge and data access, with a senior marketing leader as sponsor. Add IT or security for governance and a sales or service counterpart for shared data. MIT CISR also recommends assembling senior technical and data leaders to set the current stage and target.
Reassess quarterly in year one, then twice a year once scores stabilize. The field moves fast: McKinsey found 44% of organizations now report scaling AI across the enterprise, up from 38% a year earlier . Reassess after any big change, like a new agent, a CRM migration, or a policy update.
This AI maturity index is the article’s practical assessment framework, not an official HubSpot metric. Score each dimension from 1 to 4:
Add the scores for a quick read: 6 to 10 is Early, 11 to 15 is Emerging, 16 to 20 is Established, and 21 to 24 is Transformational. Then apply the cap rule: your effective stage can’t sit more than one level above your lowest dimension. A team that scores 4 on use cases and 1 on governance has a risk problem, not a Transformational program. The lowest dimension is your binding constraint, so invest there next.
If you can’t produce the artifact, score the dimension one level lower.
The AI maturity curve rises fastest when teams stop adding tools and build a repeatable cycle. Loop Marketing helps teams move from AI pilots to measured, repeatable workflows through four stages: Express, Tailor, Amplify, and Evolve. AI supports the people in the loop; it doesn’t replace their judgment.
McKinsey’s findings point the same way. Nearly three-quarters of high performers report fundamentally redesigning workflows because of AI, versus about one-quarter of other respondents , and they’re twice as likely to have defined processes for measuring impact.
Shadow AI grows when people lack an approved option that works. Inventory every tool in use, including free ones. Publish a short approved-tools list, assign an owner to each use case, and make the approved path the easiest one. Review quarterly and retire overlapping tools. Sprawl also hides cost: about one in five organizations say AI operating costs constrain their AI use .
Data quality sets the ceiling for AI results. HubSpot’s cross-functional study found 74% of companies that use AI and have excellent data also beat revenue targets . That shows correlation, not cause, but it matches the pattern that AI amplifies whatever data it gets.
Data readiness comes down to five practices: accurate, deduplicated records; clear field definitions; documented consent and permissions; role-based access; and a named data quality owner. Smart CRM unifies customer information in one place and includes a centralized audit log of actions taken by people, automations, integrations, and AI.
Trust is a real concern as 29% of marketers cite trust, privacy, or security as their biggest personal challenge with AI. Privacy rules vary by region. If you market to people in the EU or UK, review what the GDPR requires with your legal team. This article isn’t legal advice.
McKinsey found that high performers work to mitigate more AI-related risks than other organizations do . Governance and results tend to rise together.
Smart CRM provides connected customer context for relevant activation and measurement, so the record that informs a personalized email also feeds the report that shows whether it worked. In McKinsey’s survey, revenue gains from AI are most often reported in marketing and sales .
Agent use is growing: over 85% of surveyed marketing departments use AI agents , and 77% use at least two. More automation means more places for an unmeasured error to compound.
Start measurement with the lead nurturing metrics you already track, then add review time, error rate, and cost per output. To see how your numbers compare, get the 2026 State of AI in Marketing Report .
Attribution has limits. Marketing influences deals through many touches, so a lift in one metric doesn’t prove the AI workflow caused a revenue change. Report lift against the metric the workflow targets, run tests long enough to smooth out noise, and call results directional until a test repeats.
Teams at the top of the curve beat MQL and CAC targets at higher rates, and McKinsey’s data shows the small group of high performers pairs AI with redesigned workflows, leadership commitment, and defined measurement . Start with one workflow, one owner, and one metric.
Ready to benchmark your team? Download the 2026 State of AI in Marketing Report .
It depends on your binding constraint, and no published benchmark gives a reliable timeline. As a planning assumption, expect one or two quarters per level for a single workflow when the constraint is process (ownership, documentation, measurement). Data and governance constraints take longer because they involve other teams.
A marketing operations or revenue operations leader should own the day-to-day roadmap, with a senior marketing leader as sponsor. Governance needs shared ownership with IT, security, and legal. Name one owner per workflow.
Track three things: your index score by dimension each quarter, one outcome metric per AI workflow, and the share of workflows with documented evidence. Use before-and-after comparisons or a simple holdout. A spreadsheet is enough to start.
Keep one shared inventory of AI use cases across marketing, sales, and service, and run them from one source of customer data. Hold a monthly review where owners share results and reuse prompts, workflows, and policies.
Upskill when your binding constraint is a skill your current team can learn within a quarter or two, such as prompting, tool fluency, workflow design, or reviewing AI output. Hire when the constraint is a specialized skill you can’t build quickly, such as data engineering, marketing operations, or AI governance, or when no one has the capacity to own the work.
Check your lowest-scoring dimension in the AI maturity index first. If it points to a people gap, match the fix to how fast you need to move.
